title: Money in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain the three jobs money does: a way to pay, a measure of value and a way to save.
summary: Money is anything that does three jobs: a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes did all three.

cards.headline: In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes became money. Even non-smokers wanted them.
cards.body: Economist R. A. Radford was a prisoner there, and in 1945 he explained why. Cigarettes were doing the three jobs that make something money. Learn those three jobs and you know what money is.

cards.headline: Job 1: a way to pay
cards.body: Trade in the camp began as barter: my jam for your biscuits, if we each wanted what the other had. Then cigarettes took over. Everyone, non-smokers included, would sell for cigarettes, because they could spend them later on something else. That's a medium of exchange: something you accept not to use, but to pass on.

cards.headline: Job 2: a measure of value
cards.body: Soon every price in camp was quoted in cigarettes. Prisoners called out offers like "cheese for seven", and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment. Nobody had to work out what cheese was worth in jam. One common unit let anyone compare anything. That's a unit of account, the ruler you measure value with. Yours is probably dollars, euros or pounds.

cards.fact: Money you can smoke is a risky way to save.
cards.context: Job 3 is store of value: money should keep until you're ready to spend it. Prisoners did save cigarettes in reserve. The flaw? People also smoked them. When deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. The camp's savings had literally gone up in smoke.

mascot.line: Now you have all three jobs: a way to pay, a measure of value, a way to save. The whole tree builds on them.

cards.headline: Money: defined
learned: Medium of exchange: accepted so you can spend it again
Unit of account: the ruler for prices
Store of value: it keeps until you spend it

questions.prompt: Which list names the three jobs money does?

options.label: A way to earn, a way to spend, a way to give
options.rationale: Earning and giving use money, but the three jobs are paying, measuring and saving.

options.label: A way to pay, a measure of value, a way to save
Coins, banknotes and bank balances
options.rationale: Those are forms money takes, not the jobs it does.

options.label: A way to borrow, a way to tax, a way to lend
options.rationale: Those all use money, but they aren't its three jobs.

questions.explanation: Money is a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

questions.prompt: Why would a non-smoker in Radford's camp sell food for cigarettes?

options.label: Guards ordered everyone to trade in cigarettes
options.rationale: Nobody ordered it: cigarettes took over through trading.

options.label: Non-smokers planned to take up smoking
options.rationale: They wanted cigarettes to spend, not to smoke.

options.label: They could spend the cigarettes later on something else
Red Cross parcels held nothing but cigarettes
options.rationale: Parcels also held food like jam, biscuits and chocolate.

questions.explanation: Cigarettes had become a medium of exchange: people took them because others would take them in turn.

questions.prompt: A café menu lists every item in dollars. Which camp habit did the same job?

options.label: Saving cigarettes in reserve
options.rationale: That's storing value, the third job.

options.label: Smoking the cigarettes
options.rationale: That uses cigarettes up; it doesn't measure anything.

options.label: Swapping jam directly for biscuits
options.rationale: That's barter, with no common unit.

questions.explanation: Dollars on a menu and cigarettes in the camp both give every price one common unit: they're units of account.
